svg.text: Post-operative complications: the day tells you the diagnosis
A post-operative fever, read by timing
Day 0 to 2
Lungs
Atelectasis — shallow breathing, not clearing secretions
Day 3 to 5
Urine
Urinary infection, often catheter-associated
Day 4 to 6
Veins
Deep vein thrombosis — calf pain, swelling, warmth
Day 5 to 7
Wound
Surgical site infection — redness, heat, pus, pain increasing
Memory hook: wind, water, walking, wound — in that order through the first week.
WOUND DEHISCENCE
The wound edges separate, often around day 5
to 8, frequently heralded by a sudden gush
of serous pink fluid from the wound.
Cover with a sterile saline-soaked dressing,
lie the patient flat, call the surgeon.
EVISCERATION
Abdominal contents protrude through the
wound. This is a surgical emergency.
NEVER push the organs back in.
Cover with sterile saline gauze, keep it moist,
knees flexed, nil by mouth, prepare for theatre.
Why early mobilisation and deep breathing matter more than any drug
Lying still after surgery causes three of the four complications above: the lung bases collapse, the calf veins
stagnate and clot, and the bladder is not emptied properly.
Getting the patient sitting, breathing deeply and walking is the single most effective post-operative intervention.
Adequate pain relief is what makes it possible — an unmedicated patient will not breathe deeply or walk.
